title: Delhi High Court Upholds Seven-Year Jail Terms in 2020 Riots Death Case
excerpt: Justice Madhu Jain dismissed appeals by five men convicted of culpable homicide, holding they led an armed mob and that failure to identify the fatal blow does not absolve an unlawful assembly.
body:
• The Delhi High Court on October 27 upheld seven-year rigorous imprisonment for five men convicted over the death of a 22-year-old man during the February 2020 north-east Delhi riots.
  • Justice Madhu Jain held the men were at the forefront of an armed mob exhorting others to assault the victim, not merely present in the crowd.
  • The court ruled that failure to identify which mob member inflicted the fatal head injury does not absolve members of an unlawful assembly under Section 149 of the IPC.
  • The trial court had convicted them on November 30, 2024, under Sections 148 and 304 Part I, and sentenced them on January 13, 2025, with a fine of Rs 30,000.

The Delhi High Court has upheld the conviction and seven-year jail term of five men for culpable homicide not amounting to murder in connection with the killing of a 22-year-old man during the communal riots in north-east Delhi in February 2020. Justice Madhu Jain dismissed the appeals filed by Aman Kashyap, Devinder Kumar, Pradeep Rai, Ashish and Arun Kumar, affirming the judgment of the Additional Sessions Judge at Karkardooma Courts. Bar and Bench reported that the High Court found the evidence showed more than the mere presence of the appellants in a crowd.

What the court found

The case arose from FIR No. 87/2020 registered at Dayalpur police station after the victim was chased and assaulted by a mob near Brijpuri and Chand Bagh on February 25, 2020. He was taken to Guru Teg Bahadur Hospital, where he died. The post-mortem attributed death to shock resulting from ante-mortem brain injuries caused by blunt-force impact, according to Law Trend.

https://x.com/NH_India/status/2115362764705378421

The High Court relied on the testimony of a beat constable, identified as PW-10, who placed all five men at the forefront of the armed mob and said they exhorted others to assault the victim. Other police personnel described the pursuit and the assault continuing even after the man had fallen near police barricades. On that evidence, the court concluded the assembly shared an unlawful common object of assaulting the victim and causing him bodily harm.

"The deceased was pursued, surrounded and assaulted even after he had fallen near the police barricades."

— Delhi High Court, Justice Madhu Jain

Why the appeals failed

The convicts argued that eyewitness accounts were inconsistent, that police statements were recorded late, that independent witnesses did not support the prosecution, and that no test identification parade was held. The court rejected those challenges. It held that the absence of a test identification parade does not automatically invalidate identification evidence, and that police witnesses cannot be discarded only because of their official status.

The central legal point concerned Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, which fixes liability on members of an unlawful assembly. The appellants argued they could not be held liable because the prosecution could not prove which person inflicted the fatal injury. The court held that once membership of the unlawful assembly and its common object are established, the absence of proof identifying the individual author of the fatal injuries does not by itself absolve the accused. At the same time, it clarified that mere presence in a gathering, without the requisite common object or knowledge, is not enough to invoke Section 149.

Background and what follows

The trial court convicted the five on November 30, 2024, under Section 148, rioting while armed with a deadly weapon, and Section 304 Part I, culpable homicide not amounting to murder, read with Section 149. It sentenced them on January 13, 2025, to seven years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs 30,000. The High Court upheld both the conviction judgment and the sentencing order insofar as these five appellants are concerned, in Sessions Case No. 199/2021.

The ruling closes the High Court stage for these five convicts in this FIR, one of the many cases arising from the February 2020 violence in north-east Delhi. Any further challenge would lie to the Supreme Court. For families following the long-running riot cases from abroad, the judgment is a reminder that trials and appeals from 2020 are still working through the courts more than six years later, with liability in mob cases turning on common object and active participation rather than on identifying a single fatal blow.
